Miami

Also find this entry through: Myaamia / Miami

Miami is a broader people name with distinct community and government routes. This small path concentrates on the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma’s Myaamia Center partnership, archival language work and the Removal Project’s introduction to the 1846 Wabash Valley removal; it is not a guide to every Miami community.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and homelands

Myaamia people have homelands in the Great Lakes and Miami river systems, with communities continuing in Indiana and Oklahoma.

Read the sources [1] Miami University

02

Historical context

Many were forcibly removed from Indiana in 1846, later moving again from Kansas to Indian Territory.

Read the sources [1] Miami University

03

Living communities and further study

The Myaamia Center is a Miami Tribe of Oklahoma initiative supporting language, culture, knowledge, and education within a university partnership.

Read the sources [2] miami-oxford.org (publisher not verified)

04

A particular community–university partnership

The Myaamia Center identifies itself as an initiative of the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma within Miami University. The University’s timeline records the Project’s creation in 2001 and its later development into a Center. This institutional relationship belongs within a broader history that also includes separately represented Miami communities.

Read the sources [3] Myaamia Center / Miami University [1] Miami University

05

Archives as resources for language learning

The Center’s Language Research Office explains how analysis and digitization of older dictionaries and notes feed community language programmes. Its Education Office describes a portal and curriculum intended to reach learners in different places. These are explanations of methods and educational aims, not measurements of every learner’s experience.

Read the sources [4] Myaamia Center / Miami University

06

A route into the 1846 removal records

The Removal Project’s introduction describes forced movement from the Wabash River Valley to Kansas in 1846. It explains how student and Center work produced transcriptions of correspondence. Begin with that context before treating an individual document as representative. The modern Wabash bridge image introduces a regional setting, not a documented removal crossing.

Read the sources [5] Myaamia Removal Project / Miami University Libraries

History — selected Miami Tribe–University relationship timeline ↗

Miami University’s timeline records milestones in its relationship with the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma. The selected entries concern this institutional partnership, not a complete history of the broader Miami people.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual timeline entries from 1991–2022, reader lines120–193: heritage students, creation of the Myaamia Project, later Center and commemorations.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Public HTML body read normally. Earlier portions, underlying agreements, interviews and programme outcomes were not independently reviewed; an institutional anniversary is not evidence of universal community agreement.

About the Myaamia Center — mission and community setting ↗

The Center describes itself as a Miami Tribe of Oklahoma initiative within an academic setting, developing language and cultural resources for community use. This is a specific partnership’s own description.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual mission, community-learning and support body, reader lines117–130. Logo explanation was encountered but no logo or claimed traditional motif is reproduced.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Public HTML body read. Linked classes, visits, educational materials, participant experiences and outcomes were not inspected. The Center’s institutional voice does not stand for every Miami government or person.

https://miamioh.edu/centers-institutes/myaamia-center/about/

Offices within the Myaamia Center — selected language and education projects ↗

Selected office descriptions explain how archival language research supports learning, and how educational materials reach a geographically dispersed community. Read these as the Center’s project explanations, not independent outcome evaluations.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual Language Research body lines140–153 and Education body159–174: dictionary/ILDA work, education portal, heritage curriculum and land-record research introduction.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Public HTML body read normally. Original dictionaries, manuscripts, ILDA records, login-based lessons, linked maps and underlying land records were not inspected. Project goals, quantities and upload status are not independently verified.

Academic / referenceMyaamia Removal Project / Miami University LibrariesSource 5

About the Myaamia Removal Project — historical introduction and document method ↗

The project introduces the 1846 forced removal from the Wabash River Valley and explains its work making correspondence more accessible. The project introduction is distinct from the original letters it links.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual substantial indexed main body: removal introduction, month-long movement to Kansas, and explanation of student/Center transcription from Office of Indian Affairs microfilm roll418.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Substantial indexed page body was read; a later ordinary reader request returned502. No complete individual letter, microfilm image, treaty or full archive was inspected. The modern Wabash photograph provides regional context, not proof of a historical crossing point.

https://myaamia.lib.miamioh.edu/s/removal/page/about
